paper_title: Terminal π–π stacking determines three-dimensional molecular packing and isotropic charge transport in an A–π–A electron acceptor for non-fullerene organic solar cells

qa_pairs.question: What is the molecular architecture and composition of the electron acceptor ITIC?
qa_pairs.answer: ITIC is a fused-ring electron acceptor (FREA) that utilizes an A-π-A molecular architecture. This structure consists of a central fused-ring backbone flanked by terminal indenedione (IC) acceptor units.
qa_pairs.source_title: Terminal π–π stacking determines three-dimensional molecular packing and isotropic charge transport in an A–π–A electron acceptor for non-fullerene organic solar cells

qa_pairs.question: Describe the molecular packing arrangement found in ITIC single crystals.
qa_pairs.answer: The ITIC single crystal exhibits a one-dimensional edge-to-face stacking structure. In this arrangement, two nonequivalent molecules (A and B) alternate along the b crystallographic axis, with the backbone edge of one molecule embedded between the pendant phenyl groups of the adjacent molecule.
qa_pairs.source_title: Terminal π–π stacking determines three-dimensional molecular packing and isotropic charge transport in an A–π–A electron acceptor for non-fullerene organic solar cells

qa_pairs.question: Why does ITIC form 3D molecular packing in thin films rather than backbone-to-backbone π–π stacking?
qa_pairs.answer: In ITIC thin films, 3D molecular packing is driven by local π–π stacking between the terminal IC acceptor units. Stacking between the fused-ring backbones is inhibited by the large steric hindrance created by the four alkyl phenyl groups attached to the backbone.
qa_pairs.source_title: Terminal π–π stacking determines three-dimensional molecular packing and isotropic charge transport in an A–π–A electron acceptor for non-fullerene organic solar cells

qa_pairs.question: How does the electron mobility of ITIC thin films compare to its single-crystal form, and what is the nature of charge transport in each?
qa_pairs.answer: The electron mobility of ITIC in thin films is approximately 1.46 × 10⁻³ cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹, which is nearly double the mobility of its single-crystal form (7.4 × 10⁻⁴ cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹). Furthermore, thin films exhibit isotropic charge transport across three dimensions, whereas single crystals show highly anisotropic transport primarily along the b-axis.
qa_pairs.source_title: Terminal π–π stacking determines three-dimensional molecular packing and isotropic charge transport in an A–π–A electron acceptor for non-fullerene organic solar cells

qa_pairs.question: What specific evidence from radial distribution function (RDF) analysis confirms the π–π stacking distance in ITIC films?
qa_pairs.answer: Radial distribution function (RDF) analysis of simulated ITIC films shows a distinct peak at approximately 0.37 nm for the center-of-mass of the terminal IC groups. This specific peak confirms the presence of local π–π stacking between these terminal units.
qa_pairs.source_title: Terminal π–π stacking determines three-dimensional molecular packing and isotropic charge transport in an A–π–A electron acceptor for non-fullerene organic solar cells

qa_pairs.question: Compare the electronic coupling values of the terminal IC-IC stacks in ITIC films to the dominant packing mode in ITIC crystals.
qa_pairs.answer: The average electronic coupling for terminal IC-IC π–π stacks in ITIC films is 18.4 meV. This is significantly higher than the 10.8 meV coupling observed in the dominant packing mode (P_AB) of the ITIC single crystal.
qa_pairs.source_title: Terminal π–π stacking determines three-dimensional molecular packing and isotropic charge transport in an A–π–A electron acceptor for non-fullerene organic solar cells

qa_pairs.question: How does the thin-film electron mobility of the non-fullerene acceptor ITIC compare to the fullerene derivative PC71BM?
qa_pairs.answer: The fullerene derivative PC71BM exhibits a higher thin-film electron mobility of approximately 6.6 × 10⁻³ cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹ compared to the non-fullerene acceptor ITIC, which has a mobility of approximately 1.46 × 10⁻³ cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹.
qa_pairs.source_title: Terminal π–π stacking determines three-dimensional molecular packing and isotropic charge transport in an A–π–A electron acceptor for non-fullerene organic solar cells

qa_pairs.question: What molecular design strategy is suggested to enhance the electron mobility of A-π-A fused-ring electron acceptors like ITIC?
qa_pairs.answer: To improve electron mobility, it is necessary to finely tune the terminal acceptor units to increase local intermolecular π–π interactions. A key part of this strategy is to enhance the LUMO distribution on these terminal units to increase the resulting electronic coupling in the π–π stacks.
qa_pairs.source_title: Terminal π–π stacking determines three-dimensional molecular packing and isotropic charge transport in an A–π–A electron acceptor for non-fullerene organic solar cells
